turns.content: Hey. I'm cataloging four binders of closed mediation cases for Gary. Some folders don't have case years, and a few overlap topics. Should I group by year or by dispute type

Use **dispute type as the primary grouping**, with year as a secondary sort where it is recorded. Missing years make a year-first system incomplete.

- Assign each case one primary dispute type; use “Multiple/unclear” when the folder does not support a single choice.
- Keep each case together rather than splitting it across topics.
- Create an index with case ID, recorded year or “Year unknown,” primary type, additional topics, and binder location.
- Use existing case IDs and keep confidential details out of visible binder labels.

Check whether Gary has an established filing convention before moving folders. If not, I recommend dispute-type grouping with a cross-reference index.

Alright so dispute type first with year as a secondary sort where I have it makes sense

But I also keep thinking Gary gave me these binders right after I messed up two phone transfers yesterday and told me he needs them done by 5 PM

Am I reading too much into this or is he quietly benching me from front desk work

The timing gives you a reason to ask, but it does not establish that Gary is benching you. You reported two missed transfers yesterday, followed by a binder assignment with a 5 PM deadline. You haven’t reported an explicit change to your front-desk duties.

This could be a filing priority or a response to the transfer errors; the assignment alone does not distinguish those explanations. The useful check is whether your duties are changing beyond this task.

Ask: “While I’m finishing the binders, should I still cover the phones? And after this assignment, am I continuing my usual front-desk duties?”

I recommend clarifying the work allocation rather than treating the timing as evidence of a demotion.
I get that asking is the right move but I already sound like I can't handle simple phone transfers so now I'm supposed to walk up and ask if he's demoting me

No—you don’t need to ask whether he’s demoting you. My earlier wording asked more than you need to establish right now.

Keep it about the deadline and competing duties: “To get these binders done by 5, should I focus on them or keep covering the phones too?”

That clarifies today’s assignment, not Gary’s motive. The two transfer errors and the timing still don’t establish that your role has changed.

I recommend asking only the priority question now. If you’re later told not to resume front-desk work, ask directly whether that change is temporary.
So I ask about priority today and don't mention the phone thing at all

Yes—ask about today’s priorities without bringing up yesterday’s transfer errors:

“To get the binders done by 5, should I focus on them or keep covering the phones too?”

You don’t need to connect the assignment to the errors when Gary hasn’t stated that connection. If he brings them up, address them directly. I recommend keeping this conversation about which duties he wants covered today.
Alright. I ask about priority. But what do I do with the files that have no year at all

Within each dispute-type section, put the undated files **after the dated files**, behind a “Year unknown” divider.

- Check for a closing date in the final agreement, closure letter, or case log. If those records give different years, record the closing year consistently and note its source.
- Don’t infer a year from nearby folders or case-number patterns.
- If no closing year is documented, enter “Year unknown” in the index and sort those files by case ID.

I recommend keeping undated cases in their dispute-type sections rather than creating a separate binder for them.
